sections.title: Get started
sections.intro: Four steps from nothing to your first command. You only need a server for the ticket commands; the GitHub commands work on their own.

items.title: 1. Install
items.note: macOS with Homebrew. Windows, Linux and direct downloads are in the CLI README.

items.title: 2. Make a token
items.note: Open API tokens and create one named for whoever will use it (for example claude-code). Choose kind Agent for an automated tool, and tick only the scopes it needs. A token can never do more than you can, and it is shown once.

items.title: 3. Connect
items.note: Copy the token, then run this. It reads your clipboard, so the token never lands in your shell history or on screen. Don't copy anything else in between.

items.title: Which server am I using?
items.note: Shows the server the CLI talks to.

items.title: Something not working?
items.note: Checks your installation and credential store. It never touches the network or any secret.

sections.title: Tickets
sections.intro: References look like SD-12. Columns are fixed for everyone: backlog, todo, in_progress, in_review, test, done, canceled.

items.title: List tickets
items.note: Filter by status or assignee. Add --limit to see more.

items.title: See one ticket
items.note: Shows its trail, its subtasks (with their pull requests and CI), and any linked pull requests.

items.title: Create a ticket
items.command: sled-dog ticket create "Fix login redirect" --priority high --body "What is wrong and why it matters"

items.title: Change a ticket
items.note: GitHub sync moves tickets for you as pull requests open and merge (draft: in progress, open: in review, merged: test). Move one by hand only when sync cannot know. Moving test to done is a person's call.

items.title: Assign a ticket
items.note: Use an empty string to unassign.

sections.title: Finding and archiving
sections.intro: Finished tickets leave the board after a while (the workspace owner sets how long, in days or business days). They are never deleted, and search always finds them.

items.title: Search everything
items.note: Finds tickets that mention every word, in the reference, title, description, assignee, subtasks, trail steps or pull request titles. Best matches come first, and each result says why it matched. Archived tickets are included.

items.title: Search for an exact phrase
items.note: Quote words to keep them together. Without quotes every word must appear, in any order.

items.title: Jump to a ticket or subtask
items.note: A reference finds that ticket first; SD-12.2 finds ticket 12 only if it has a subtask 2.

items.title: Narrow a search
items.note: Filter by status or assignee. Add --live to hide archived tickets, or --archived to see only those.
items.command: sled-dog ticket search checkout --status done --assignee baden

items.title: Browse the archive
items.note: ticket list shows the board by default. --archived shows only archived tickets; --all shows both.

items.title: Archive a finished ticket
items.note: Only a done or canceled ticket can be archived. It leaves the board but keeps its subtasks, trail and pull requests. Tickets also archive themselves once they have been closed long enough. --dry-run checks without changing anything.

items.title: Bring a ticket back
items.note: Its closing time restarts, so it is not archived again at once. Moving a ticket out of done also brings it back to the board.

sections.title: Linking pull requests
sections.intro: Sync reads your pull requests and links them to tickets by reference. How you name things decides what links.

items.title: Name the branch and title after the ticket
items.note: Any reference in the branch name or the pull request title links it: a branch like SD-12-fix-login, a title like "SD-12: Fix login redirect". For a subtask use SD-12.2-api. These always link.

items.title: In the description, use a keyword
items.note: A reference in the description links only after closes, fixes, resolves, part of, or refs, as in "Closes SD-12" or "Part of SD-12". A plain mention ("see SD-12", "follow-up in SD-12.2") does not link, so talking about related work never attaches it by accident.

items.title: Pull GitHub now
items.note: The server syncs every few minutes by itself. Run this to catch up right away. A repository source sees a new pull request immediately. An organization source reads GitHub's search, which can trail a brand-new pull request by a few seconds, and sync says so if it finds nothing.

sections.title: Subtasks
sections.intro: When one ticket needs several pull requests, split it. The ticket follows its subtasks: it moves to in review, test or done only when every subtask has, so one early pull request cannot carry the whole ticket forward.

items.title: Add a subtask
items.note: It gets a reference like SD-12.1. Numbers are never reused.
items.command: sled-dog subtask add SD-12 "API changes" --assignee baden

sections.title: The trail
sections.intro: A trail is a ticket's ordered checkpoints: design, copy, approvals, QA. Anyone a checkpoint is assigned to (or anyone on its team) can complete it, even with a read-only role. Address a step by its number in ticket view or by its name.

items.title: Add a checkpoint
items.note: Give a team or a person by name. A name that fits two people is refused instead of guessed.
items.command: sled-dog step add SD-12 Design --team Design

items.title: Assign a checkpoint
items.note: A team or a person; assigning one clears the other. Use --unassign to clear both.

sections.title: GitHub on its own
sections.intro: These work without a Sled Dog server. They read your pull requests and builds straight from GitHub (github.com or Enterprise).

items.title: Connect to GitHub
items.note: Paste a personal access token when asked (nothing shows as you type). Add --host for Enterprise.

items.title: Switch account
items.note: For people with more than one GitHub account or host.

items.title: Sign out
items.note: Removes the saved credentials for that account from this machine.

items.title: One pull request, and its builds

sections.title: Recipes
sections.intro: The commands above, in the order you will actually use them.

items.title: Start a piece of work
items.note: Make the ticket, then branch from it. Open the pull request with the reference in its title, and sync moves the ticket to in review.
items.command: sled-dog ticket create "Add CSV export" --priority medium

items.title: Split work across pull requests
items.note: Add one subtask per pull request, then name each branch after its subtask (SD-13.1-api, SD-13.2-ui). The ticket stays in progress until the last of them reaches review.

items.title: Check before you change
items.note: --dry-run asks the server to validate the change and say what would happen, including whether the parent ticket would move. Nothing is written.

sections.title: For agents and scripts
sections.intro: Every command is built to be driven by a program as well as a person.

items.title: Machine-readable output
items.note: --json prints exactly one document: schema_version, data, meta and errors. Nothing else goes to stdout, and there are no colors or progress bars.

items.title: Retry safely
items.note: Creating something sends an idempotency key. If a call is retried with the same key you get the original back instead of a duplicate. One is generated for you and printed in meta; pass your own to control it.

items.title: Pick the server without logging in
items.note: For automation, set these instead of running login. SLED_DOG_API_TOKEN overrides the saved token and is never stored. The server URL must be HTTPS (plain http is allowed only for localhost).

items.title: When something unexpected happens
items.note: An internal error names the exception type (a type field in JSON). Set SLED_DOG_DEBUG=1 to print the traceback to stderr; stdout stays a single JSON document. Review a traceback before sharing it.

exitCodes.meaning: Something failed, or the thing you asked for was not found
Invalid arguments: a bad reference, an unknown name, a missing field. Nothing was written
Not signed in, or not allowed. The message says which, and why
